narrative:
The model estimates a 42% chance that you will not pass your final year. That is below an even chance, but it is still a substantial risk, and it is why you are being required to take remedial courses rather than proceed without support.

The strongest reason the model leaned toward failing is your intention about higher education: you indicated you do not want to continue to higher education, while every student who passed in the comparison group did want to. Not planning for further study was the top factor pushing the prediction toward failing. Two other factors pushed in the opposite direction, toward passing, but were not strong enough to outweigh that concern. Your record of no past class failures was the second most influential factor and helped your case, since the average passing student also had none. Your travel time of 30–60 minutes was the third most influential factor and also slightly helped your pass estimate, even though only about 5% of passing students had such a long commute.

To improve your position, focus first on your final-year goals and ask how remedial courses connect to passing and to any future study or training. Keep your no-failure record intact, and use the family support and internet access you already have. Since you study less than two hours weekly, while most passing students study two to five hours, build a regular study routine and speak with your guardian and teachers about a realistic plan.
